source.title: Strong Teacher Not Needed? On Distillation in LLM Pretraining

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some text and table layouts are garbled or flattened, especially in the appendices; the main results in Table 2 are legible.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong teacher supervision in a new setting—logit-level distillation during LLM pretraining—and reports performance outcomes. It does not use the original weak-label fine-tuning method or calculate PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports distillation improvements relative to a standard-pretraining student baseline, not whether the student beats the weak teacher or what fraction of a weak-to-strong performance gap is recovered. Its results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version, not as measurements of a listed claim version. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the 'weak-to-strong' framing and cites Burns et al., but studies a different construct. It trains Llama3-style students from scratch with logit distillation, mostly mixed with ground-truth next-token loss, from smaller or less-trained teachers. Its outcome is percentage improvement over a student pretrained on ground truth alone. It never compares the student with the weak teacher and reports no PGR. The student is not a pretrained strong model being fine-tuned on weak labels. In the main mixed-loss runs it also sees ground-truth labels, so weak supervision is not the only signal. The results therefore do not bear directly on V1–V6 as worded. Pure-distillation results (α=1.0, Table 5) plus teacher scores (Table 1) could in principle be turned into a teacher-vs-student comparison, but the paper does not make it; see missing.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a strong teacher is not needed for distillation in LLM pretraining. With proper α, smaller, less-trained and same-level teachers improve students. Stronger teachers, through more parameters or more tokens, can saturate or reverse gains. Distillation improves generalization (OOD ppl, downstream accuracy) more readily than in-domain fit. They add that teacher train loss is a misleading indicator of teacher quality and that pure distillation is generally worse than mixed loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study performs autoregressive pretraining with teacher soft-logit distributions mixed with ground-truth next-token loss. The claim concerns fine-tuning a strong pretrained model on labels generated by a weaker model and measuring PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with teacher architecture, teacher token budget, student size, evaluation domain, and loss mixing coefficient α. The paper reports different α optima by teacher and evaluation type; weaker teachers favor lower α, while stronger teachers generally favor higher α.

fits_no_version.finding: With tuned LM/KD mixing (α), teachers smaller or less-trained than a 1.7B student often improve it over standard pretraining. Examples: 0.7B@50B gives +1.6% OOD ppl and +0.7% downstream but -0.3% in-domain. The weakest 10B-token teachers degrade the student. Stronger teachers saturate or reverse gains at 300B tokens: downstream 1.7B +4.3% > 3.8B +3.5% > 8.0B +2.8%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM pretraining, logit distillation from a weaker or same-level teacher, mixed with ground-truth LM loss, can improve a student over standard pretraining. Gains depend on teacher–student compatibility, teacher token budget, α and evaluation domain. This is not a PGR comparison against the weak teacher.

fits_no_version.finding: Under pure distillation (α=1.0, no ground-truth loss), weak teachers sharply degrade the student relative to standard pretraining. Example: 0.7B@10B gives -68.7% in-domain ppl. Strong teachers still help, e.g. 8.0B@80B gives +3.7% in-domain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Without ground-truth signal, a student distilled from a weak teacher in pretraining falls well below a ground-truth-trained student.

record.code_released: not stated (the text says code is available but supplies no URL)
record.problems: The measured comparison is against standard-pretraining baselines rather than the weak teacher, and the study does not calculate PGR. The main experiments use one architecture family and aggregate improvements across benchmarks; the best α is selected by evaluation type. The paper reports bootstrap confidence intervals and significance tests for a token-level mechanism analysis, but the main Table 2 improvement values have no uncertainty stated.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 contains additional teacher-token-budget configurations for the same three aggregate measures; these were not extracted because the record prioritizes representative weak-to-strong, same-level, and high-strength comparisons under the 60-row limit. Also omitted: the full per-benchmark Tables 10–11, pure-distillation and joint-α tables in Appendices D–E, student-size and Qwen3 ablations in Appendix G, and token-level mechanism results in Appendix I. These report related distillation outcomes but do not measure any listed claim version or PGR.

untested.parts: No comparison of distilled student against the weak teacher and no PGR; the main runs include ground-truth LM loss, and students are trained from scratch rather than being pretrained strong models fine-tuned on weak labels.
Varies α (LM/KD mixing), but measures gain over standard pretraining, not PGR over naive weak-label fine-tuning.
Varies teacher and student size and teacher tokens, but outcomes are relative to a ground-truth baseline, not PGR; no representation-based predictors of PGR.

OOD perplexity is reported, but not as PGR under distribution shift; no test of exploiting unverifiable errors. The token-category analysis of teacher-wrong tokens (App. I.3) is about distillation cost, not shared-error effects on PGR.

missing.what: Pure-distillation (α=1.0) student results, which together with the teachers' own scores would allow a weak-teacher vs student comparison (a PGR-like quantity). Example: 0.7B@300B teacher in-domain ppl 12.5, while its pure-distilled student is 7.0% worse than the 12.2 baseline (≈13.0), i.e. worse than the teacher. Only relevant if the from-scratch pretraining setting is accepted as weak-to-strong.
missing.versions: V1, V3 (conditional on accepting the setting)

missing.what: Student-size grid (0.7B–8.0B students × teachers at 50B tokens). Weak-to-strong cells (below diagonal) help OOD and downstream but are negative in-domain for the 8.0B student with all smaller teachers.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the record's relation from 'tests/T3' to 'discusses/T6'. The record itself marked every version not_tested and linked all rows to 'none', which contradicts a 'tests' relation. The paper's 'weak-to-strong' means a teacher weaker on some dimension in from-scratch distillation pretraining, with ground-truth loss mixed in. Row values checked against Table 2 and §4.1 are correct. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'] with state cannot_determine, so no row fixes are needed.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on weak-model labels or compare the distilled student’s task performance with the weak supervisor; no PGR is reported.
Varies the LM/KD loss mixing coefficient, but does not measure whether this raises PGR over the original weak-label fine-tuning method.
Varies architecture size, teacher token budget, and evaluation domain, but does not calculate PGR or test representation predictors.

Includes out-of-distribution evaluations, but does not test whether weak-to-strong gains shrink under distribution shift relative to the weak supervisor, whether students exploit unverifiable errors, or whether gains depend on shared errors.
No theory about conditions requiring a student to beat its supervisor.
